title: The Night the Numbers Came In
gateMessage: The nation votes today. You cannot look away from this.
location: National Counting Center — Ashenmere Exhibition Hall

narrative.text: The side room at the national counting center smells of coffee and anxiety. The full cabinet is here — not because anyone required them to be, but because no one wanted to be anywhere else. Marić has his hands folded on the table, his knuckles pale. Vostane is staring at projected figures that someone printed three hours ago and that are already obsolete. Dusek is standing by the window, watching nothing in particular, her posture exactly the same as it is during military briefings. Nobody is talking. The radio on the side table crackles with the voice of the national broadcaster: Thornfeld at fifty-eight percent turnout, Dravenhollow at seventy-one.

You enter. Nobody says anything. The silence continues for one moment longer than is comfortable — long enough for every person in the room to register your arrival and decide collectively that someone else should be the first to speak. Then Marić exhales.
He does not sound surprised. He sounds like a man who has been waiting to say it out loud so that someone else could be responsible for deciding what it means.

He pauses. The pause is longer than it needs to be. That is how Vyktor delivers bad news — not by saying it, but by letting the silence around it grow until you fill it with the worst thing you can imagine. He knows that what you will imagine is usually worse than what he is about to say. He is usually right.
I thought you should know before the room fills up.

He turns. The clipboard is covered in numbers written in his own handwriting — neat, precise, the hand of a man who has been tracking political margins since before you were elected and will be tracking them long after. The rural districts are underperforming. The urban districts are holding. The Dravenni precincts are voting at rates no one predicted. Whether that means enthusiasm for the constitution or desperation for something — anything — to change, no one in this building can say for certain.

Theron is in the back room with the legal team. He is already drafting contingency statements. Three versions — landslide, narrow win, and 'the counting will continue tomorrow.' He insists that preparation is not pessimism. I am not sure he believes that.

The main hall is beginning to fill. Journalists. Observers. MPs who have been waiting for this night since the constitutional process started fourteen weeks ago. The international press has sent correspondents — the Arcturian and Orythian papers will both run front-page pieces tomorrow, regardless of what happens. You have about thirty minutes before you need to be in front of cameras. You have about thirty minutes to decide what you are going to say if the constitution fails.

The constitution is more than a legal document. It is the thing you will be remembered for — or the thing that will be remembered as your failure. If it passes, everything else you do this term becomes possible. If it fails, everything else becomes irrelevant. The margin does not even matter. Pass is pass. Fail is fail. History does not grade on a curve.

Vyktor hands you the clipboard. The numbers are not final. They will not be final for hours. But you can already see the shape of the result forming, like a photograph developing in chemical solution — not yet clear enough to name, but clear enough to know that whatever emerges will change everything.

monologue: The numbers are not final. Nothing I do right now will change the count. But everything I do right now will be remembered — by the people counting, by the people watching, by the people who will write about tonight for the rest of their lives.

choices.text: Wait for the full count. Democracy is patient. You should be too.

reactions.text: Dorven Province reporting shortly. Kravenstal in 40 minutes. Should have a projection by midnight.

He appears in the doorway, a folded sheet of paper in his hand. Patience is the least practiced of democratic virtues, he says, almost to himself. It is also the most essential. One cannot rush a nation's conscience.

choices.text: Address the crowd outside — rally support for the constitution while you wait.

reactions.text: Crowd is four thousand and growing. Security recommends 10-minute address maximum. Say nothing you would not want on the front page of the Herald in 14-point type.

Theron pauses by the window, looking down at the crowd below. They have been out there since the polls closed. Some of them since the polls opened. The constitution is a document of law, but it is also a document of hope. Tonight they need the hope. The law can wait until morning.

choices.text: Prepare your closest advisors for either outcome — hope for the best, plan for the worst.

reactions.text: He turns to the legal team. Whatever happens, we cannot look surprised. Surprise looks like incompetence.

Theron nods — three slow dips of the head that seem to take him further from the room with each one. He has been preparing for both outcomes since the day he drafted the first article. Preparation is not pessimism. It is the discipline that makes hope possible.

choices.text: Ask the Archbishop to lead a prayer for the nation — whatever happens, the people need to see unity.

reactions.text: He looks at you for a moment longer than necessary. Church attendance up 4 points. The Archbishop will appreciate the gesture. So will Thornfeld. And so will the 72 percent of this country that still attends services weekly. He pauses. Not a political calculation. Merely a political observation.

Theron removes his glasses. The constitution, he says quietly, is built on the assumption that democracy is sufficient. It is not. Democracy is necessary. But it must be held together by something deeper than procedure. Tonight we remind the country what that something is. I am grateful the Chancellor understands this.
